transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Martinez: Hey everyone good afternoon, thanks for joining, we'll do quick round of updates on the quantization POC. um Daniel, do you want to kick off with the latest numbers?
[00:22] Daniel Hsu: Yeah sure. So we reran the INT8 profile with the updated calibration table, using the micro-batch size of 8, and we saw latency drop about 2.8x at 512 tokens on the transformer benchmark, throughput roughly 1.9x higher. CPU overhead for preprocessing is nil. FP8 runs are showing similar latency to INT8 but slightly less variance, interestingly.
[00:48] Priya Rao: Sorry can you repeat the delta for me, the 2.8x is compared to fp32 right?
[00:54] Daniel Hsu: Yep fp32 baseline. INT8 gave ~2.8x lower p99 latency, and FP8 was around 2.4x but with tighter p95/p99. The per-token cost dropped by about 45% on INT8, FP8 was about 40% lower.
[01:18] Marcus Lee: Quick question on quality—what are we seeing on end-task metrics? Our classification thresholds are pretty sensitive.
[01:26] Daniel Hsu: Right so we ran the eval set you gave us. For INT8 the avg accuracy delta was -0.6% on the classification task, F1 drop of about -0.8. Perplexity moved by +0.9. For FP8 the metrics were mostly within noise: accuracy -0.1%, F1 -0.2, perplexity +0.2.
[01:55] Elena Gomez: hmm that's, that's within our acceptable band for inference cost, but the edge cases are where INT8 got word swaps sometimes, we saw a few hallucinations on longer prompts.
[02:08] Daniel Hsu: Yeah we observed some tokenization edge cases interacting with the quantization—particular attention on layernorm and attention softmax precision. We suspect a couple of attention heads are more sensitive, can do selective per-layer FP16 or mixed quant.
[02:28] Tom Baker: Any noticeable difference in KV cache behavior? We care about streaming chat SLOs.
[02:33] Daniel Hsu: KV cache was stable; there was slight increase in memory jitter with INT8 but within thresholds. FP8 had smoother allocation. The runtime's continuous batching and prefix caching still gave consistent latency. There might have been a mis-transcribe earlier, the notes called it KV "cash" in places.
[02:52] Priya Rao: On deploy modes, if we go dedicated how different are these numbers? We have concerns about capacity and cost.
[03:00] Sofia Martinez: Good point. The Dedicated runs with reserved GPU pools generally show similar quantization gains, but because we can tune kernel selection and compilation flags at deploy-time, you'll often see an extra 5-10% latency improvement vs noisy multi-tenant hosted. Daniel, remind them about kernel pinning?
[03:17] Daniel Hsu: Sure. On dedicated we can pin optimized kernels and enable longer continuous batches without noisy neighbor interference—so effective p99 is better. Also, we can flip on more aggressive fusion and use precompiled kernels for INT8 which helps.
[03:34] Marcus Lee: Security quick question—where are the logs for these runs stored and retention? We need to check for audit and SOC2.
[03:40] Liam O'Connor: We store run logs in customer-isolated buckets for private and dedicated customers, retention is configurable; default for POC is 30 days. We'll share the security one-pager and SOC2 summary after the call.
[03:56] Priya Rao: On the calibration—what's the recommended approach? We tried a small sample and saw variance.
[04:02] Daniel Hsu: Use a representative corpus, about 5-10k tokens per typical prompt shape—run the calibration notebook we provided. Also try per-layer calibration and post-calibration fine-tuning with a small labeled set if you need to recover micro-accuracy. For your use-case where thresholds matter, Daniel (sic) suggested doing selective FP16 on top N sensitive layers.
[04:26] Priya Rao: Are there automated tools in Redwood to identify sensitive heads/layers?
[04:30] Daniel Hsu: We have a diagnostic script that outputs per-head sensitivity scores; we'll include it. It flags layers where quantization causes token divergence beyond a set threshold.
[04:40] Marcus Lee: For the FP8 run we want to validate end-to-end with our pre- and post-processing, we'll run 1k queries as Daniel suggested and upload results. If FP8 holds then we prefer FP8 for lower variance.
[04:52] Sofia Martinez: Sounds good. On pricing implications, INT8 gives larger cost savings but with slightly more QA risk; FP8 is a good middle ground since your accuracy delta is small. We'll send a delta pricing sheet showing per-token costs at current commit tiers.
[05:08] Tom Baker: Any gotchas with micro-batching for streaming workloads? We saw some increases in tail latency with larger micro-batches.
[05:14] Daniel Hsu: Yep, micro-batch size is a trade-off. For streaming chat, keep micro-batch to 1-4 for lower tail latency; for high throughput batched inference you can push to 8-16. We used 8 in the INT8 runs for batched benchmarks.
[05:30] Priya Rao: Could we test with micro-batch 4 on the same INT8 profile to see p99 impact?
[05:36] Daniel Hsu: Absolutely, we'll run that as part of the next benchmark. We'll share the config.
[05:42] Marcus Lee: Also we want to confirm fallback strategy—if INT8 fails QA in production, what's the runtime behavior?
[05:48] Sofia Martinez: We support policy-driven fallbacks: route to FP8 or FP16 model variant automatically, and can do canary rollouts. We can wire in an automatic regression detector to pause rollouts if eval metrics dip beyond thresholds.
[06:03] Elena Gomez: One more item—when you share logs please include the kernel names and compilation flags; NVIDIA's profiler team asked for that when we worked with Triton.
[06:12] Daniel Hsu: We'll include that. We'll also put in the micro-batch and kernel pinning flags.
[06:20] Sofia Martinez: Ok let's recap. Next steps: Redwood shares calibrated benchmark spreadsheet and raw logs + calibration notebook by Thursday (6/18). Acme runs FP8 1k query suite and uploads results by Mon (6/22). We schedule a dedicated-small test week of 6/23 to validate latency SLOs. Pricing delta and security one-pager to be shared.
[06:44] Marcus Lee: Sounds good, thanks all.
[06:48] Priya Rao: Thanks, talk soon.
[06:50] Sofia Martinez: Thanks everyone, end.
